paragraphs.heading: What it describes
paragraphs.text: An electron configuration tells you how the electrons of an atom or molecule are spread out among its orbitals. Take neon: its configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶, so its 1s, 2s and 2p subshells hold two, two and six electrons. The picture treats each electron as moving on its own in an orbital, feeling an average field set up by the nuclei and all the other electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Quantum mechanics ties a level of energy to each configuration. Under some conditions an electron can switch to another configuration by giving off or taking in a quantum of energy, a photon. Knowing configurations helps make sense of the periodic table, the chemical bonds between atoms, the formulas of compounds and the shapes of molecules. In bulk materials the same idea helps explain lasers and semiconductors.

paragraphs.heading: Shells
paragraphs.text: The idea was first worked out under the Bohr model of the atom. Even after later advances in understanding electrons, talk of shells and subshells is still common. A shell groups together all the allowed states with one value of the principal quantum number, n, the whole number written before each orbital letter. The nth shell can hold 2n² electrons: two in the first, eight in the second, eighteen in the third. The factor of two comes from electron spin, since each orbital takes at most two electrons, one spin up and one spin down.

paragraphs.heading: Subshells and their letters
paragraphs.text: Inside a shell, a subshell is the set of states with the same azimuthal quantum number, l, which runs from 0 up to n − 1. The values l = 0, 1, 2, 3 get the letters s, p, d and f, so the 3d subshell has n = 3 and l = 2. A subshell holds at most 2(2l + 1) electrons, which means two in s, six in p and ten in d. These limits come from quantum mechanics, especially the Pauli exclusion principle: no two electrons in one atom can share all four quantum numbers. The letters are left over from an old way of sorting spectral lines as sharp, principal, diffuse and fundamental.

paragraphs.heading: Writing it down
paragraphs.text: The standard notation lists the subshells in a row and puts each one's electron count as a superscript. Hydrogen has a single electron, sitting in the first shell's s orbital, so it is 1s¹. Lithium has two electrons in 1s and one in the higher-energy 2s, so it is 1s² 2s¹. Phosphorus, atomic number 15, comes out as 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³.

paragraphs.heading: A noble gas shortcut
paragraphs.text: For atoms with many electrons the full list gets long, so a shorter form is used. The inner electrons match the noble gas of the period before, and that part is written as the gas's symbol in brackets. Phosphorus differs from neon only by having a third shell, so it becomes [Ne] 3s² 3p³. This is handy because the electrons in the outermost shell do the most to decide an element's chemistry.

paragraphs.heading: The order is a choice
paragraphs.text: The order of orbitals in a written configuration is not fully fixed, because only how many electrons each orbital holds has physical meaning. Titanium's ground state can be written [Ar] 4s² 3d² or [Ar] 3d² 4s². The first follows the Madelung rule, where 4s fills before 3d going from argon to titanium. The second groups orbitals by n, which is the reverse of the order in which electrons leave as the atom forms positive ions.
